deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is part of Riemann's essay 'Mechanik des Ohres', published posthumously by Henle in 1867 and included in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke. In this section Riemann estimates how small the vibrations transmitted by the middle ear can be. The previous page set up a scale of sound intensities modelled on stellar magnitudes. Each magnitude step divides the mechanical energy by 10. Energy goes as amplitude squared, so the amplitude falls by a factor sqrt(10) per step. Magnitudes 1, 3, 5, 7 therefore have amplitudes in the ratio 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000.

This page is mostly qualitative argument, with one implicit quantitative step.

(a) Riemann rejects the idea that the tympanic membrane damps loud sounds through a continually varying tension, i.e. a reflex of the tensor tympani muscle analogous to the pupil adjusting to illumination. He allows protective reflexes against dangerous bangs. But he sees nothing in auditory sensation analogous to the brightness level of the visual field. He also sees no use, for the exact perception of a piece of music, in a continually varying reflex action of the m. tensor tympani.

(b) He therefore assumes that the middle ear transmits linearly with a fixed ratio. Write x_s for the stapes footplate displacement and x_a for the air displacement in front of the eardrum. Then x_s = k * x_a, with k the same for a sound heard 10 ft from a sentry as for one heard 20,000 ft away.

(c) Implicit step (mine; it is completed on the next page): for a spherical wave from a point source, amplitude goes as 1/r. So x_a(10 ft) / x_a(20000 ft) = 20000/10 = 2000. With k constant, the same ratio 2000 holds for the stapes motion.

(d) Robustness remark: even if one admits a fairly large variability of membrane tension, k only changes by a modest factor. The order-of-magnitude conclusion is unaffected.

(e) The next page completes the argument. If the stapes motion at 10 ft is just visible to the naked eye, then the motion at 20,000 ft would be just visible under 2000-fold magnification. The corresponding energy ratio is 2000^2 = 4*10^6.
errors: No error on this page itself. The 1/r amplitude law, and hence the factor 2000, is left implicit; it is valid for free spherical propagation and ignores absorption, ground effects and wind. That is acceptable for an order-of-magnitude argument.

Context note on the previous page: '1/10,000000' (10^-7) for the 'sixth' magnitude is inconsistent with a factor 10 per magnitude, which gives 10^-5 for the sixth. It is also inconsistent with an amplitude of 1/1000 for the seventh, which corresponds to energy 10^-6. Either the magnitude numeral is misread or Riemann slipped.

results.what: Assumption of linear, constant-ratio transmission of the middle ear (no adaptive damping by the tensor tympani for ordinary sounds); amplitude scaling with distance gives a ratio of 2000 between 10 ft and 20,000 ft
results.modern_name: Linear middle-ear transfer function; inverse-distance law for spherical sound waves; contrast with the acoustic (stapedius/tensor tympani) reflex
results.usually_credited_to: Inverse-distance law is classical (18th–19th c. acoustics); the middle-ear reflex debate is associated with Johannes Müller, Helmholtz and Politzer

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to Riemann's known, published (1867) 'Mechanik des Ohres'. The content is a qualitative physiological argument plus an elementary inverse-distance scaling estimate.

checkable.asserts: amplitude ratio between 10 ft and 20,000 ft under the 1/r law
amplitude ratios for magnitudes 1, 3, 5, 7 when energy drops by 10 per magnitude (context from the previous page)
energy for magnitude 6 is 10^-5, not 10^-7 as written on the previous page

'Verhältniß{+x+}' marks an insertion/footnote sign (x) after 'Verhältniß', not a letter of the word.
